title: Awakening
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Here's a summary paragraph summarizing the main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk: The talk emphasizes the importance of turning one's attention inward to awaken to the true nature of reality, rather than trying to control or separate from it. This involves recognizing the cycle of suffering that arises from our conditioning and reactions, and learning to pause and choose a more mindful response. By cultivating awareness of our thoughts, emotions, and sensations through mindfulness practice, we can develop a greater understanding of ourselves and approach life with a more open and accepting mindset.

sentences.text: The person who gives the dharma talk today is one of our Home Priests, Ryushin Kate McKenna.
I'm really looking forward to what she has to say about our awakening.
Thank you so much, Kate, for giving the talk today.
I'll get myself situated here.
This is so strange, looking at yourself.
I think I'm gonna switch and look at all of you.
*All right.
An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Well, thank you, everybody, for being here, for taking time on a Sunday, a lovely Sunday morning, and sharing the dharma together.
And thanks, Chris, for orchestrating this whole affair.
And also to Tim.
I don't think he's here today, but thanks for having the glue to keep the whole process together.
I'm going to start with a quote here.

*You should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.
Body and mind of themselves will drop away, and your original face will be manifest.*
As many of you know, these are the words of our 13th century founding teacher from Japan, Eihei Dogen.
I've been chewing on them for a while, just trying to open them up and see what it means to actually apply them.
How can we use them when we're sitting, and how do we make them meaningful in our daily lives?
On the surface, of course, it does seem clear enough that Dogen is advising us against getting too caught up in our heads.
He's telling us not to confuse our words and our thinking and our narratives, our ideologies, with what's happening right in front of us.
There's a saying from the Shurangama Sutra that says, a finger pointing to the moon is not the moon.

In other words, the teachings, the study, the words might describe the path or awakening, or Buddha nature, but we mustn't mistake them for the unmistakable, unspeakable reality that we're trying to express.
Then Dogen tells us to turn our light inwardly, to illuminate ourselves.
Of course, illuminating ourselves does not mean putting ourselves in the spotlight, situated at the center of the universe.
So the backward step is not stepping back from life to observe it, separating ourselves as subject from object.
Rather, we're stepping back into life to merge with it, and we're allowing life to step forward to meet us.
As Dogen puts it, the myriad things come forward and illuminate the self.
And he says that this is what awakening is.
The early Buddhists gave us many ways to show us how to do this.
They also pointed out many traps leading us to serious misconceptions about ourselves and the world.
Many of these teachings were on the causes, the effects, and the cycles leading to our sense of separation and our sense of suffering.
One of these maps is called the 12 links of causation.
It's also called the 12 nidanas.
Each link in this causal chain is the result of a previous one and then the cause of the next.
I'm going to list these, but please don't worry about remembering them.
I'm mostly just going to be talking about one of them, the one that you'll hear translated as feeling.
So these are the links: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name and form, the six senses, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth and death.
And then the cycle just starts all over again and goes back to ignorance.
I have to admit that I found the teachings on the nidanas somewhat perplexing.
Sometimes they really seem too tidy and too simplistic, and other times they seem too complex.
I also found a number of different interpretations for some of these links, particularly formations.
Some teachers presented the links as happening in a very linear, sequential way, and they assumed rebirth.
Some saw the causes and effects as happening simultaneously, and some saw them happening from moment to moment in our daily life.
To top it off, they seem to culminate in gloom, like one miserable life after another.
But then I found this article entitled The Buddhist Twelve Nidanas for Dummies, and I thought, oh, this is cool, I'm going to get it.
It was comforting just to know there are other people who felt the same way I did, but it really wasn't too helpful.
Still, this teaching did seem very important to early Buddhists.
Before I rejected it, I needed to understand why it could have been so important to them.
I also needed to know how the teaching could be useful and applied to practice and also to life.
Now, a couple of things were really clear about the links.
They were not trying to tell us how gloomy existence is, but rather to show us how to get out of the gloom.
They were telling us that if we could cut a link in this chain of cause and effect, we could break the addictive cycle of suffering that we're caught in.
They tell us that there are multiple and complex causes and conditions that result in suffering.
Some of these we can't change and some of them we can.
We can have some power to address and take responsibility for the course of our lives.
And at the same time, we can be helpful to others.
But then finally, I encountered Norman Fischer's interpretation of these nidanas, and that really helped me to better understand the 12 links.
It also helped me apply Dogen's advice to take a backward step.
First of all, Norman simplified and reduced these 12 links into only four factors, and I'll try to briefly summarize what Norman had to say about them.
His first factor he calls the tragedy of consciousness.
When I first read this word, tragedy, it seemed like a really strong word and it almost stunned me.
It never occurred to me to think of consciousness itself as tragic.
But here's why.
With this first factor he reduces the first three nidanas of ignorance, formations, and consciousness to simply consciousness.
That helped.
It's consciousness itself, Norman says, that's the ultimate cause of suffering.
In order to operate, consciousness has to involve separation.
To be conscious of something we have to stand outside of it.
Norman says to hear a bird, I have to be distanced from it.
To see the sky, I have to be other than the sky.
Consciousness, he says, is inherently in need of healing.
It brings alienation.
Alienation brings exile, longing, and fear.
He goes on, all religions agree that this is a fundamental problem.
Norman's second group of factors summarizes the next three nidanas, the ones called form, the six senses, and contact.
Generally these are references to the material world.
Norman says that these factors cause us to, quote, enter a partial world.
When we see with our alienated consciousness, this world is no longer us.
We are no longer it.
Entering this partial world is an inevitable consequence of birth and the emergence of consciousness.
It can't be avoided.
I'm going to take a little bird walk here.
I have my own interpretation of the second factor.
After I walked away from Catholicism, I reenvisioned the Bible, and in this case, it was the story of Adam and Eve.
Adam and Eve were banished from the garden after eating the forbidden fruit of knowledge, which I find that word interesting here.
It was a knowledge that allowed them to funnel and to limit this cosmos, the whole cosmos, and themselves through this narrow world of ideas and concepts.
With this view, the notion arose of an individual self, an egoic identity with the me at the center of the universe looking out.
This construction of a self was helpful for human ascendancy and for survival and for acquiring what we humans biologically required.
It did give us a certain sense of control.
But what was designed to help us meet the threats of harm and injury simultaneously cut us off from a more expansive view of reality, or from our own Buddha nature.
This led to our fall from the garden, the fall that Norman called a tragedy and the Christians called original sin.
Both of them called for redemption and a return to our original state.
So I'm going to weave back to Norman here.
The third stage, Norman calls reacting to this partial world.
It's his summary of the last three nidanas of feeling, craving, and grasping.
The world has a heavy impact on us, and in this world, we have choices to make.
Each choice is limiting, and it brings mixed consequences with it.
So we react, and our reactions inevitably bring trouble, disappointment, and conflict.
We keep pushing.
We keep making efforts to control our world, but they're often futile.
And if we're successful for a while, we fear that our good fortune will eventually change.
And it probably will.
So we live our lives grasping onto what we have, trying to get more or to rid ourselves of what we don't want.
The Garden of Eden has been lost.
Adam and Eve have now become hooked to their egoic identities.
And as the Bible says, they've covered their nakedness.
Their original face, their Buddha nature, is now hidden.
They toil and sweat and live their lives in competition.
Norman's fourth group of factors he calls living and dying.
These factors summarize the last three nidanas of becoming, birth, and death.
I'm going to just quote this directly from Norman.
*If consciousness were never produced, and if we in the world were not partial, there would just be one wholeness, ever-transforming, ever-peaceful.
There would be no choices to make, and no resulting actions with reactions.
But thanks to consciousness, we are born.
And because we are born, we die.*
So that's Norman's summary of the twelve links, and here's my little summary of Norman's summary.
It goes like this.
There's consciousness and birth.
Accompanying consciousness is the tragedy of separation.
We feel the alienation between self and the world.
This is dukkha, the first of Buddha's four noble truths, the existential fact of suffering.
Pleasant experiences inevitably change, nothing lasts.
But we keep trying to orchestrate the world to the tune we want.
In the meantime, our neighbor has a different score and his neighbor yet another.
And then we wonder why the song of the world can sometimes feel so discordant.
If we're given only the first two truths of suffering and its causes, it would appear that we're doomed to this endless cycle.
Unfortunately, this isn't the case.
More than 2,500 years ago, the Buddha appears, and he gives us some hope.
His third and fourth noble truths tell us that there is a possibility and a path to liberation.
He tells us that there can be an end to suffering.
Since then, our Buddhist ancestors have been telling us that there is what Norman calls a pivot point, or what I'm taking to be a backward step that we can take within these 12 links of causation.

Although we can't stop consciousness and birth, and the appearance of this partial world, there is a place where we can stop this repetitive cycle of discontent, a place where we can intervene in our experience, and where deep insight and freedom can emerge.
This is the sixth link in the chain of 12, and it's called contact.
That's the very first place that we can have some influence and exercise some choice.
Here, we can interrupt the cycle at the point of what's called in Sanskrit vedana.
In English, it's often referred to as feeling.
If you've chanted the Heart Sutra many times, and most of you have here, then you've heard of vedana many times, and you might not have known it.
When we recite, *no form, no sensation, no perception, no formation, no consciousness*, you hear the word sensation.
This is an alternate translation for vedana.
You also might hear it called feeling tone, or tonality, or hedonic tone.
And in some Tibetan traditions, they refer to it as intrinsic knowing.
The word sensation to me seems to fit this experience most accurately.
When we use the word feeling, we're generally referring to our emotions, but that's not what's indicated here.
Emotional states are much more complex than vedana.

Instead, vedana is the condition that occurs when our sense organs, our sight, sound, smell, et cetera, and in Buddhism we have six of them, including consciousness, initially come into contact with objects, people, or events in the world, and a barely conscious awareness of this interaction arises.
So sense organ meets the object of the senses.
It emerges as a gut reaction, deep in the body, mind, and heart, and Norman says this can be a foundation of a new identity if we can bring awareness to it.
If we can stay mindful and present with these sensations, with our simple momentary experience, there's another kind of subtle recognition that happens.
We'll sense the encounter as either pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral.
Either we like it, we don't like it, or maybe we're apathetic or disengaged from the experience.
Any experience can produce this.

Simply the whiff of a flower, maybe an inflection in a person's voice, a horn honking in traffic, but it could also be something major, like a shock, an accident, or a birth on the positive side, maybe.
Once we've recognized it as pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral, we've landed on this pivot point.

With attention, we can pause, we can take the backward step, and in that pause, we have the freedom to choose our response to the experience and move toward liberation and avoid a thoughtless reaction.
Because it's such an early link in this chain, snapping it here can prevent other automatic and habitual responses that kickstart the cycle of thoughts and emotions that lead to suffering.
But if we miss it, our minds latch on.
We lurch forward to cling to or grasp what we experience as pleasant, or tighten up and contract and push away the unpleasant.
Or if it's neutral, we might not know what to do, and we're stupefied or in denial.
Either way, our minds are buffeted back and forth like billiard balls reacting to whatever hit us last.

Then our assumptions and mixed-up views about the world proliferate, and we find ourselves in the throes of the classic three Buddhist poisons of attraction, aversion, and ignorance, and even more heightened states of greed, anxiety, anger, confusion, all leading to suffering for others and ourselves.

So the sooner we detect our response to Vedana, the more we can determine the direction we take toward these three poisons: whether it will lead us toward liberation or sink us further into our egoic identity.
I don't know if Bob's here, I can't tell, but some of you have taken some of the Goenka trainings, and he's a big fan of Vedana.
He was a 20th century Vipassana meditation teacher, originally from India, and he's no longer alive.
But here's what he had to say about Vedana.
He says:
*This discovery of the Buddha, that the real cause of tanha, and tanha means grasping or aversion, lies in Vedana.
This is the unparalleled gift of the Buddha to humanity.
With this one discovery, he gave us the key to open the door of liberation within ourselves.

Among the many meditation techniques of India and other parts of the world that I have come across, or have heard about, there is none like this that goes to the root causes of suffering and eradicates them.*
So that's a pretty strong endorsement.

If we do manage to stay present with a pleasant or unpleasant sensation without chasing after it, turning away from it, or blaming it on someone else, we might see that our response has nothing to do with the event.
Rather, it's about the impact that the pleasant or unpleasant event has had on us.
If we look deeply at our immediate experience, we can see that there's really no inherent value in the object or event our senses are coming into contact with.
They're empty of value.
They're neither good nor bad in themselves, and it's only our reactions that make them seem this way.
I want to do a little thought experiment with you.
Think about your first love or first crush, or just any deep love you might have had for someone.
She or he is perfect, a dream, and this will last forever, and then you move in together.
He's on his phone all night, he's eating you out of house and home, he's borrowing your money, and all of a sudden you don't love him anymore.
But he hasn't changed.
Your likes and dislikes have.
Or what about body odor?
Your own's not so bad, but what about the sweaty guy sitting next to you on the bus?
So it's the quality of the contact, the pleasantness around pleasantness.
That quality doesn't reside in the person, the object or event, as we tend to think it does.
It comes from our own histories, our own social conditioning and opinions that we've accumulated through our lifetime and through countless generations before, no doubt.
And as Dogen says, *once the least like or dislike arises, the mind is lost in confusion.* But before we edit this programming and all our pros and cons, the encounter is bare.
It's, as we say, just this, in its basic purity.
Becoming aware of Vedana can prevent our past from soiling the present, the future, and also the lives of others.
Like a lot of the practices that we study, it's helpful to start with a conceptual understanding of Vedana.
But then we do need to apply Dogen's words and take the backwards step and cease from intellectual understanding.
So just feel into it.
When you note a reaction to a sensation, don't start psychoanalyzing yourself.
Like, "Oh, I don't like this because my mother always forced me to eat Brussels sprouts."
No, just check in with the body for a direct experiential lead.
Although it may sometimes tell us things we don't like, the body never deceives us.
In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha tells us that we can sense this tendency to like or dislike in both the body and the mind.
But he does spend a long time talking about the body, and he does give it a primary role.
And in the Fukanzazengi, Dogen's instructions for Zazen are also mostly about the body, and he includes even our physical environment.
He tells us: eat moderately, sit on a thick mat, adjust your leg positions, your hands, align the parts of your body, like the nose to the navel and shoulder to the hips.
Position your tongue, keep your eyes open, and then take a deep breath.
And think not thinking.
Keep returning to the breath and the body, as we're trying to do.
Just stop dwelling on past and future and go back to this primary present sensation.
Our Zazen is a really ideal space to attend Vedana in a number of ways.
Here, we can watch our inhalations or exhalations and notice what subtle reactions, or maybe no reactions, arise with each.
Or we can even be systematic with this.
Start with a complete body scan, feeling sensations one by one as we move attention from head to toe.

I've been practicing with this by going from chakra to chakra, and seeing what I discover about my pleasant or unpleasant responses as I find some openings in some chakras and then some blockages at different points.
Or we can also just sit and connect with sensations as they pop into awareness, or feel the aliveness of the body as a whole.
Pain or discomfort, both emotional and physical, can also be a particularly good focus for Vedana.
Pain really gets our attention.
It's not as subtle as the others I've been talking about, and our don't-like and resistant minds are quick to react to it.
I have personally found that staying with discomfort can be a really powerful teacher.

One of the things I've seen is that when I direct the breath into the area of pain, and this is particularly true for me in sesshin, I sometimes bring up old grief and occasionally I cry, tears that really needed to be shed.
It's also brought up old stories of shame and inadequacy.
But in Zazen, we're free to sit with all this stuff, right, and connect with these painful narratives and then gently breathe them away.
The weight really does lessen, and also the tendency to identify with them.
On the other hand, we might be pain-free, sitting in our peacefully perfect full lotus, and we might start wallowing in our self-satisfaction.
That's the other end of the spectrum.
But if we can simply listen to our pain or our pleasure as we would to a good friend, we'll see the frames of our mind change and continually arise and pass away.
Even if the pain doesn't go completely away, and I've noticed it really often does, the sensation takes on a more expansive quality.
The pain itself could still be grumbling, but the who behind the pain is not.
And then the next time we sit, we'll know better how to work with the pain.
Maybe we better get off the cushion and start sitting on a chair, or whatever kind of adaptation we might need to make.
But going back to Norman here again, this insight into Vedana is not easy to come by, he says.
He says the subtlety of Vedana as it first arises can be hard to tackle, and we can still miss these delicate feeling tones.
And of course, even in zazen, you know how natural it is to find our thinking overriding our senses.
But here's the good news: it's never too late.
There are other links in the chain that we can latch onto even if we miss the first whiff.
Our likes and dislikes can be detected in every moment of experience, physical, mental, subtle, gross.
So even when we drift off into thought, we can still investigate our reactions, our likes and dislikes as they relate to our thoughts and projections.
We are heavily into the body, but thoughts are useful for this as well.
Also, simply labeling the encounter, saying to ourselves this sensation is pleasant or unpleasant or neutral, can help us pause and attend.
Or we can identify it with just the word "thinking," or if it's an emotional experience, "feeling."
This is a very simple technique and a very simple response, but I have really found it helpful.
For me, the simpler the technique, the better.
And then try treating each of these arisings the same as you would if you heard a bird chirping outside.
Why would we assign a higher value to a bird song than we do to a thought or an emotion?
All of them are gifts of consciousness, and they're really miracles.
And all of them soon to pass away, as we know.
So when you greet them in this way, they fall naturally in their own time.
I like to use the metaphor or the image of ripe fruit just falling from the tree, just natural, no struggle, no resistance, just letting gravity do the work.
So the next step is taking this awareness of our likes and dislikes beyond the cushion and out into our daily lives.
I decided to take my likes and dislikes grocery shopping to Fred Meyers.
I figured that was a pretty busy place, and a great place to have some reactivity.
So that's why I chose Fred Meyers.
On this first trip, I decided to watch my dislikes, and there were a bunch of them.
For example, why were Bob's old fashioned oats on the baking aisle instead of the cereal aisle where I wanted them to be?
And why aren't there any more of my very necessary chocolate mocha cliff bars?
But what was most annoying was this recording of a female voice at the self checkout station.
I don't know if you've been to places where you do the self checkout and they've got this recorded voice.
Anyway, she insisted on telling me what to do.
Even though I had packed my groceries, she kept insisting that I place an item in my bag.
She starts out nice enough: "Place your item in the bag."
But then her voice seemed to rise to a crescendo, or so I was imagining anyway, each time she prompted me.
By the third "place your item in the bag," I was talking back to the voice: "I have placed my item in the bag."
By this time the attendant is standing behind me, listening to me talk to myself, or her.
It was a little embarrassing.
But I went back again.
The next time to shop, I decided to note my likes, and there were also plenty of them.
On the way there, just noticing the sky was delightful.
While looking at the houses, I noticed my subtle reactions to all the different colors.
Just something like color can trigger this pleasant, unpleasant, or likes and dislikes reaction.
And when I finally got to the store, the clerk seemed so helpful.
When all the cabbages were too big, the produce fellow even stopped his stocking and cut one in half for me.
But best of all, and this is wonderful, the recorded voice at the self-checkout station only goaded me once to put my items in the bag.
So these pleasant encounters are happening all the time, but it took refocusing my lens to appreciate them.
The point here is that it's helpful to move beyond the cushion with our awareness of likes and dislikes and neutral reactions and just apply our practice to our daily lives.
But these were minor encounters.
Other times we may have grown to work with feelings that have gotten out of hand already.
They may have grown over the months and the years into pretty demonic beings.
In fact, in working with Vedana, I have found it really helpful to start with something big and painful, or something I have a strong or persistent reaction to.
Sometimes something that I really can't miss, maybe something or someone I find particularly threatening, and that's usually to my ego.
Lately, it's national events that shake up my sense of security or threaten my values.
I might find this situation or person on and off my mind during my busy daily activities.
But because I'm preoccupied with something else, I don't really attend to those feelings.
They linger there.
I get a vague sense of them that lodges in the body.
But it's not until I'm sitting in Zazen that I have the space and the quiet to notice and feel those unnamed and subtle sensations rising.
Maybe it's a surge of heat or a sudden chill, muscles contracting, a tendency to shrug up the shoulders, or tightening in the chest.
After practicing this way for a while, those sensations do become more and more obvious, and they're recognized a lot sooner.
They have less of a hold on me, especially if I'm watching at the same time these old narratives and the history that memory has attached to all of them.
I've learned over time to see them as just sensations.
Eventually, I do find that they've passed away, and I wonder how I could have been so tormented by them in the past.

So I began with Dogen's quote: *You should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.
Body and mind of themselves will drop away and your original face will be manifest.* This backward step of Vedana can be, and is, a plunge into a potential well of insight and wisdom.
As Norman said, it can be a source of a new identity.
But in taking this backward step, I want to leave you with a little cautionary note.
Practicing with Vedana, and with whatever it achieves, we remind ourselves that there's no score card.
We're not competing with ourselves or anyone else.
And behind it all, as the Heart Sutra says, there's nothing to attain, nothing to hang on to, nothing solid and permanent.
So we can let go of any strained or willful effort.
And as Shanti Deva says, we can practice like a piece of sheer cotton cloth being swayed by a wafting wind.
When we're walking backwards, we can't see where we're going.
We let our feet take us into unknown and uncharted territory, trusting that existence is already whole and complete just the way it is and that every moment will take care of itself.
So thank you, all of you, for listening, for being here.
We'll end with the Dharma chant.

*May our intention equally extend to every being and place* *With the true merit of Buddha's way* *Beings are numberless, I vow to save them* *Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them* *Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them* *Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become*
